claim: Consciousness research has used post hoc sorting of neural measurements based on observers' 'seen' and 'unseen' judgments as a hallmark approach.
source: A hallmark approach has been to ask human observers to judge stimuli as 'seen' (conscious) and 'unseen' (unconscious) and use post hoc sorting of neural measurements based these judgments.
evidence: This is stated as an established methodological approach in consciousness research.

claim: Cognitive and response biases strongly affect how observers place their criterion for judging stimuli as 'seen' versus 'unseen'.
source: Unfortunately, cognitive and response biases are known to strongly affect how observers place their criterion for judging stimuli as 'seen' versus 'unseen', thereby confounding neural measures of consciousness.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about bias effects on perceptual judgments.

claim: The effect of conservative and liberal criterion placement on neural measures of unconscious and conscious processing has never been explicitly investigated.
source: Surprisingly however, the effect of conservative and liberal criterion placement on neural measures of unconscious and conscious processing has never been explicitly investigated.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of prior research on this specific topic.

claim: Conservative criterion placement inflates effect sizes in neural measures of both conscious and unconscious processing.
source: Here, we use simulations and electrophysiological brain measurements to show that conservative criterion placement has an unintuitive consequence: rather than selectively providing a cautious estimate of conscious processing, it inflates effect sizes in neural measures of both conscious and unconscious processing, while liberal criterion placement does the reverse.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulations and empirical EEG data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Liberal criterion placement reduces effect sizes in neural measures of both conscious and unconscious processing.
source: Here, we use simulations and electrophysiological brain measurements to show that conservative criterion placement has an unintuitive consequence: rather than selectively providing a cautious estimate of conscious processing, it inflates effect sizes in neural measures of both conscious and unconscious processing, while liberal criterion placement does the reverse.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulations and empirical EEG data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Perceptual Awareness Scale (PAS) does not guard against criterion confounds.
source: The results confirm that the predicted confounding effects of criterion placement on neural measures of unconscious and conscious processing occur in empirical data, while further showing that the most widely used subjective scale, the Perceptual Awareness Scale (PAS), does not guard against criterion confounds.
evidence: This is supported by empirical data from Experiment 2 showing criterion effects on all PAS levels.

claim: The experimental context determines whether the relative confounding effect of criterion placement is larger in neural measures of either conscious or unconscious processing.
source: Follow-up simulations explicate how the experimental context determines whether the relative confounding effect of criterion placement is larger in neural measures of either conscious or unconscious processing.
evidence: This is supported by simulations showing differential effects based on sensitivity and overall criterion placement.

claim: Criterion placement threatens the construct validity of neural measures of conscious and unconscious processing.
source: We conclude that criterion placement threatens the construct validity of neural measures of conscious and unconscious processing.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the simulations and empirical data.

claim: Watson rejected introspectionism.
source: After Watson rejected introspectionism (Watson, 1914), and the cognitive revolution in turn rejected behaviorism (Baars, 1994), it has become widely accepted that there is middle ground: one can potentially gain access to (some of) the contents of the mind by asking observers to report on these contents.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Watson, 1914.

claim: The cognitive revolution rejected behaviorism.
source: After Watson rejected introspectionism (Watson, 1914), and the cognitive revolution in turn rejected behaviorism (Baars, 1994), it has become widely accepted that there is middle ground: one can potentially gain access to (some of) the contents of the mind by asking observers to report on these contents.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Baars, 1994.

claim: One can potentially gain access to some of the contents of the mind by asking observers to report on these contents.
source: After Watson rejected introspectionism (Watson, 1914), and the cognitive revolution in turn rejected behaviorism (Baars, 1994), it has become widely accepted that there is middle ground: one can potentially gain access to (some of) the contents of the mind by asking observers to report on these contents.
evidence: This is presented as a widely accepted position in psychology.

claim: The search for the neural correlate of consciousness is based on asking observers to report on the contents of their mind.
source: This idea has been the central tenet in what has come to be known as the search for the neural correlate of consciousness (Crick and Koch, 1990; LeDoux et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Crick and Koch, 1990 and LeDoux et al., 2020.

claim: To determine what consciousness is, one must contrast it with what is not conscious.
source: It was realized early on that to determine what consciousness is, one must contrast it with what is not conscious, or else the concept of consciousness is an empty shell (the contrastive approach, see Baars, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Baars, 1994 and is presented as an established principle.

claim: The contrastive approach presupposes that one can distinguish between conscious and unconscious processes.
source: This presupposes the idea that one can distinguish between conscious and unconscious processes (so-called dual process models).
evidence: This is a logical inference from the contrastive approach.

claim: The idea of unconscious inference was proposed by Helmholtz in 1867.
source: Indeed, the idea of a hidden unconscious life that precedes and/or escapes our conscious experience also has a long tradition, starting with the idea of unconscious inference (Helmholtz, 1867), and later in Sigmund Freud's hidden unconscious (Freud, 1904).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Helmholtz, 1867.

claim: Sigmund Freud proposed the concept of the hidden unconscious.
source: Indeed, the idea of a hidden unconscious life that precedes and/or escapes our conscious experience also has a long tradition, starting with the idea of unconscious inference (Helmholtz, 1867), and later in Sigmund Freud's hidden unconscious (Freud, 1904).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Freud, 1904.

claim: In the 1980s and 1990s, there was a debate about how to experimentally establish whether a stimulus has reached consciousness.
source: In the 80s and 90s of the previous century, this culminated in a heated debate centered around the question of how to experimentally establish whether a stimulus has reached consciousness or not.
evidence: This is presented as historical fact about the field.

claim: Some researchers defended the position that unconscious cognition should be determined at an objective detection threshold.
source: This debate roughly featured researchers defending the position that one should determine unconscious cognition at an objective detection threshold (Greenwald, 1992; Greenwald et al., 1996; Greenwald et al., 1989; Snodgrass et al., 2004), whereas others defended the position that only a subjectively defined threshold can establish unconscious cognition (Cheesman and Merikle, 1986; Merikle, 1992), with critical comments on the very notion of dual process models by questioning the existence of unconscious cognition at all (Holender, 1986; Holender and Duscherer, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to researchers defending this position.

claim: Some researchers defended the position that only a subjectively defined threshold can establish unconscious cognition.
source: This debate roughly featured researchers defending the position that one should determine unconscious cognition at an objective detection threshold (Greenwald, 1992; Greenwald et al., 1996; Greenwald et al., 1989; Snodgrass et al., 2004), whereas others defended the position that only a subjectively defined threshold can establish unconscious cognition (Cheesman and Merikle, 1986; Merikle, 1992), with critical comments on the very notion of dual process models by questioning the existence of unconscious cognition at all (Holender, 1986; Holender and Duscherer, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cheesman and Merikle, 1986 and Merikle, 1992.

claim: Some researchers questioned the existence of unconscious cognition.
source: This debate roughly featured researchers defending the position that one should determine unconscious cognition at an objective detection threshold (Greenwald, 1992; Greenwald et al., 1996; Greenwald et al., 1989; Snodgrass et al., 2004), whereas others defended the position that only a subjectively defined threshold can establish unconscious cognition (Cheesman and Merikle, 1986; Merikle, 1992), with critical comments on the very notion of dual process models by questioning the existence of unconscious cognition at all (Holender, 1986; Holender and Duscherer, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Holender, 1986 and Holender and Duscherer, 2004.

claim: The subjective threshold approach claims to take consciousness seriously by letting participants indicate whether they experience a stimulus.
source: The core difference between objective and subjective threshold models is that the subjective threshold approach claims to take consciousness seriously by letting the participants in a study indicate on their own terms whether they experience (see) a stimulus at a certain level of intensity (Baars, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Baars, 1994.

claim: Participants have well above-chance objective sensitivity for presentation levels at which they claim stimuli are subjectively invisible.
source: Typically, participants have well above-chance objective sensitivity for presentation levels at which they claim that stimuli are 'subjectively' invisible Stein et al., 2021) and regardless of response criterion or bias (Evans and Azzopardi, 2007; Balsdon and Azzopardi, 2015; Green and Swets, 1966).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stein et al., 2021.

claim: Objective measures align best with a scientific approach to consciousness.
source: Although objective measures seem to align best with a scientific approach to consciousness (replicable, objective, e.g. see Mei et al., 2022; Soto et al., 2019), they do require one to invoke a 'Gold Standard of seeing' that in fact does not exist (Koenderink, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mei et al., 2022 and Soto et al., 2019.

claim: Objective measures require invoking a 'Gold Standard of seeing' that does not exist.
source: Although objective measures seem to align best with a scientific approach to consciousness (replicable, objective, e.g. see Mei et al., 2022; Soto et al., 2019), they do require one to invoke a 'Gold Standard of seeing' that in fact does not exist (Koenderink, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Koenderink, 2014.

claim: Cases have been reported in which subjective experience differs even when objective performance is equated.
source: Indeed, cases have been reported in which subjective experience is reported to be different even when objective performance is equated (Fleming et al., 2010a; Hesselmann et al., 2011; Lau and Passingham, 2006; Persaud et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: Subjective measures are the measure of choice in paradigms where physical stimulation is kept identical.
source: Furthermore, subjective measures are the measure of choice in paradigms in which physical stimulation is kept identical, which are often introduced to prevent that differences between conscious and unconscious vision can be attributed to physical rather than 'mental' differences (so-called 'threshold' approaches, Sanchez et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sanchez et al., 2020.

claim: Subjective measures have been widely criticized for being confounded by effects unrelated to conscious experience.
source: Subjective measures on the other hand have been widely criticized for being confounded by effects that are unrelated to conscious experience, such as non-perceptual biases as well as regression to the mean effects (for critical reviews see Newell and Shanks, 2014; Schmidt, 2015; Shanks, 2017; Soto et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to critical reviews.

claim: Subjective measures have gained considerable popularity in consciousness research over the past 20 years.
source: Nevertheless, subjective measures have gained considerable popularity in consciousness research over the past 20 years (Dehaene et al., 2003; King et al., 2016; King and Dehaene, 2014; Lamy et al., 2009; Michel, 2022; Overgaard et al., 2010; Overgaard et al., 2006; Ramsøy and Overgaard, 2004; Salti et al., 2015; Sandberg et al., 2010; Sergent et al., 2005; Sergent and Dehaene, 2004; Soto et al., 2019; Soto et al., 2011; van Vugt et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by numerous citations to studies using subjective measures.

claim: A dominant approach in subjective threshold literature is to sort trials based on observer's responses to calculate average neural activation for 'seen' versus 'unseen' trials.
source: A dominant approach in the subjective threshold literature is to sort trials based on observer's responses to calculate the average neural activation for 'seen' (conscious) versus 'unseen' (unconscious) trials.
evidence: This is presented as an established methodological approach.

claim: Unconscious working memory has been proposed as a phenomenon based on post hoc sorting.
source: Some proposed phenomena that originate from this approach are unconscious working memory (King et al., 2016; Soto et al., 2011; Soto and Silvanto, 2014; Trübutschek et al., 2017), unconscious error detection (Charles et al., 2013), and even unconscious arithmetic (Sklar et al., 2012), for critical comments see Shanks, 2017; Stein et al., 2016.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies proposing this phenomenon.

claim: Unconscious error detection has been proposed as a phenomenon based on post hoc sorting.
source: Some proposed phenomena that originate from this approach are unconscious working memory (King et al., 2016; Soto et al., 2011; Soto and Silvanto, 2014; Trübutschek et al., 2017), unconscious error detection (Charles et al., 2013), and even unconscious arithmetic (Sklar et al., 2012), for critical comments see Shanks, 2017; Stein et al., 2016.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Charles et al., 2013.

claim: Unconscious arithmetic has been proposed as a phenomenon based on post hoc sorting.
source: Some proposed phenomena that originate from this approach are unconscious working memory (King et al., 2016; Soto et al., 2011; Soto and Silvanto, 2014; Trübutschek et al., 2017), unconscious error detection (Charles et al., 2013), and even unconscious arithmetic (Sklar et al., 2012), for critical comments see Shanks, 2017; Stein et al., 2016.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sklar et al., 2012.

claim: Arbitrary criterion placement influences the decision about stimulus absence or presence, even when consciousness of the stimulus itself is not affected.
source: Arbitrary criterion placement influences the decision about stimulus absence or presence, even when consciousness of the stimulus itself is not affected.
evidence: This is presented as a key insight about criterion effects.

claim: Two stimuli that undergo identical sensory processing and result in the same experience might be reported as seen or unseen depending on whether the observer adopts a liberal versus conservative criterion.
source: Thus, two stimuli that undergo identical sensory processing and result in the same experience might either be reported as seen or as unseen, depending on whether the observer adopts a liberal versus a conservative criterion for deciding whether the threshold for a 'stimulus present' decision was reached.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of criterion effects in signal detection theory.

claim: Perceptual decisions may be motivated by non-perceptual information such as payoff matrix or statistical regularities, even when subjective experience is not affected.
source: For example, it is well known that perceptual decisions may be motivated by non-perceptual information, such as the payoff matrix (the perceived utility of certain responses) or by statistical regularities in the environment, even when subjective experience is not affected (Rungratsameetaweemana et al., 2018; Sánchez-Fuenzalida et al., 2023b; White and Poldrack, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Roughly two thirds of consciousness researchers at ASSC conference answered that payoff-based criterion shifts do not involve changes in conscious perception.
source: Indeed, when a large group of consciousness researchers at the Association of Scientific Studies of Consciousness (ASSC) conference was asked about the relationship between payoff-based criterion shifts and conscious perception, roughly two thirds answered that they did not think that such shifts involve changes in conscious perception (Q2 in Francken et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Francken et al., 2022.

claim: The criterion problem has been known at least since the advent of signal detection theory.
source: The criterion problem has been known at least since the advent of signal detection theory (Evans and Azzopardi, 2007; Green and Swets, 1966) and has long been hypothesized to underly many – if not all – subjective threshold effects (Eriksen, 1960; Goldiamond, 1958; Peters and Lau, 2015; Phillips, 2021; Phillips, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to signal detection theory and related work.

claim: Criterion shifts have been hypothesized to underlie many or all subjective threshold effects.
source: The criterion problem has been known at least since the advent of signal detection theory (Evans and Azzopardi, 2007; Green and Swets, 1966) and has long been hypothesized to underly many – if not all – subjective threshold effects (Eriksen, 1960; Goldiamond, 1958; Peters and Lau, 2015; Phillips, 2021; Phillips, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to theoretical work.

claim: In signal detection theory, the relationship between an observer's response and the signal depends on the criterion applied to that signal.
source: In signal detection theory (Green and Swets, 1966), the relationship between the response (behavior) of an observer and the signal that the observer operates on, depends on the criterion that the observer applies to that signal.
evidence: This is a fundamental principle of signal detection theory, supported by citation.

claim: When the criterion shifts from conservative to liberal, the average signal strength within both seen and unseen response categories decreases.
source: For example, when the response criterion shifts from conservative to liberal, as is shown in the example in Figure 1A, the average signal strength within both the seen and the unseen response category decreases (see leftward diagonal lines from conservative to liberal).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1A showing the signal detection theory model.

claim: A more conservative criterion inflates neural measures of both unconscious and conscious processing when compared to a liberal criterion.
source: Somewhat counterintuitively, a more conservative criterion does not have different effects on the neural measure of 'unconscious' processing and on the neural measure of 'conscious' processing. Instead, when the two criteria are positioned symmetrically around the mean of the signal distribution as in the left panels of Figure 1B, a more conservative criterion inflates neural measures of both unconscious and conscious processing when compared to a liberal criterion (see the right panel of Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation results shown in Figure 1B.

claim: This consequence of criterion shifts on effect sizes in neural measures based on post hoc sorted trials has not been highlighted in the consciousness literature.
source: Although this consequence of criterion shifts on effect sizes in neural measures based on post hoc sorted trials is clearly implied by signal detection theory, to our knowledge it has not been highlighted in the consciousness literature.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the finding in the consciousness literature.

claim: In Experiment 1, participants viewed a continuous rapid serial visual presentation of oriented textures while EEG was collected.
source: To investigate this, we analyzed two datasets in which a criterion manipulation was applied to a detection task. In both experiments, participants viewed a continuous rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) of oriented textures while EEG was collected (see Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: The fifth texture in the sequence either contained a texture-defined square or a homogenous texture without a square.
source: The sequence of textures was always identical, except that the fifth texture either contained a texture-defined square of lines orthogonal to the background orientation (target trials) or a homogenous texture without such a square (no-target trials).
evidence: This describes the stimulus manipulation in the experiments.

claim: In Experiment 1, participants were punished with an aversive tone and monetary deduction for misses in the liberal condition.
source: To manipulate their decision criterion, they were either punished using an aversive tone with a small monetary deduction for misses (liberal condition) or an aversive tone with a small monetary deduction for false alarms (conservative condition).
evidence: This describes the criterion manipulation method in Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, participants were punished with an aversive tone and monetary deduction for false alarms in the conservative condition.
source: To manipulate their decision criterion, they were either punished using an aversive tone with a small monetary deduction for misses (liberal condition) or an aversive tone with a small monetary deduction for false alarms (conservative condition).
evidence: This describes the criterion manipulation method in Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 2, participants responded using the Perceptual Awareness Scale (PAS).
source: In a second experiment, we had a different group of participants perform the same task, this time responding using the Perceptual Awareness Scale (PAS: Ramsøy and Overgaard, 2004).
evidence: This describes the response method in Experiment 2.

claim: The PAS allows observers to indicate the strength of their experience at a fine-grained resolution ranging from 0 'No experience' to 3 'A clear experience'.
source: This scale allows observers to indicate the strength of their experience at a more fine-grained resolution ranging from [0] 'No experience' to [3] 'A clear experience' (PAS experiment, see Figure 2B and Methods for full description of the four response categories).
evidence: This describes the structure of the PAS scale.

claim: The underlying assumption of the PAS is that selecting 0 will only occur if trials are truly unseen.
source: The underlying assumption of the PAS is that selecting [0] will only occur if trials are 'truly' unseen, so that unconscious processing is not overestimated, as may happen in dichotomous or other types of scales (Overgaard et al., 2006; Overgaard and Sandberg, 2021; Sandberg et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to papers about the PAS.

claim: The PAS was developed to be impervious to non-perceptual criterion shifts.
source: The PAS was developed to be able to resolve the inability to externally calibrate subjective content, and as such its ultimate goal seems to be to be impervious to non-perceptual criterion shifts.
evidence: This is inferred from the stated purpose of the PAS.

claim: The degree to which the PAS is robust to non-perceptual criterion shifts has never been explicitly investigated.
source: However, despite its popularity, the degree to which the PAS is robust to non-perceptual criterion shifts has never been explicitly investigated.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of prior research on this topic.

claim: In Experiment 2, observers were explicitly instructed to respond in line with their experience.
source: Here, to counter criterion shifts when using the PAS, we further explicitly instructed observers to respond in line with their experience: 'Even though you receive feedback about the correctness of your responses, it is very important that you keep responding according to what you actually experience, using the Perceptual Awareness Scale. Only press 0 if you are 100% convinced that no square appeared and only press 3 if you are 100% convinced that a square appeared.'
evidence: This describes the instructions given to participants in Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 1, target presentation duration was 40 ms.
source: Aside from response mode and target presentation duration (Experiment 1: 40 ms, Experiment 2: 30 ms), both experiments were virtually identical (see Methods for other minor differences).
evidence: This is a methodological detail of Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 2, target presentation duration was 30 ms.
source: Aside from response mode and target presentation duration (Experiment 1: 40 ms, Experiment 2: 30 ms), both experiments were virtually identical (see Methods for other minor differences).
evidence: This is a methodological detail of Experiment 2.

claim: The criterion manipulation resulted in a strong criterion shift in both experiments.
source: Behaviorally, the criterion manipulation (liberal vs conservative) resulted in a strong criterion shift in both experiments, expressed in concomitant increases of both hits (responding 'seen' when a target was presented) and false alarms (responding 'seen' when no target was presented) for liberal when compared to the conservative condition (see left panels of Figure 2C, D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Sensitivity remained largely unchanged between liberal and conservative conditions in both experiments.
source: In contrast, sensitivity – simplified here as the hit rate minus the false alarm rate – remained largely unchanged (right panel of Figure 2C, D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: In Experiment 1, the criterion manipulation exerted a much larger effect on criterion (hedges g = 2.84) than on d' (hedges g = 0.30).
source: To quantify the success of the criterion manipulation in Experiment 1, we computed the signal theoretic parameter estimates criterion c (liberal: –0.30, conservative: 0.73) and sensitivity d' (liberal: 2.12, conservative: 2.39). This confirmed that the criterion manipulation in Experiment 1 was successful, and that it exerted a much larger effect on criterion (hedges g = 2.84) than on d' (hedges g = 0.30).
evidence: This is based on signal detection theory analysis of behavioral data.

claim: All levels of the PAS are affected by criterion shifts.
source: In contrast, however, we observed strong criterion shifts on all levels of the PAS, as can be seen from concomitant increases of both hits and false alarms for liberal when compared to the conservative condition (see left panels of Figure 2D), while sensitivity (collapsing PAS1, PAS2, or PAS3 as 'seen' responses) was only slightly higher for conservative compared to liberal (see the right panel of Figure 2D). This shows for the first time, that all levels of the PAS are affected by criterion shifts, questioning the construct validity of the measure (see Discussion).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from Experiment 2 shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In Experiment 2, the criterion manipulation exerted a much larger effect on criterion (hedges g = 2.02) than on d' (hedges g = 0.42).
source: Computing the corresponding signal theoretic estimates for Experiment 2 confirms this result for criterion c (liberal: –0.59, conservative: 0.60) and sensitivity d' (liberal: 1.29, conservative: 1.59). Effect sizes on these measures show that the criterion manipulation in Experiment 2 worked and that it exerted a much larger effect on criterion (hedges g = 2.02) than on d' (hedges g = 0.42), just as we observed in Experiment 1.
evidence: This is based on signal detection theory analysis of behavioral data.

claim: A linear discriminant analytic classifier was trained for each participant to discriminate target from no-target trials based on EEG data.
source: Next, to establish the effect of criterion shifts on neural measures, we turned to classification performance of EEG data as a measure of neural processing (Fahrenfort et al., 2018). First, a linear discriminant analytic (LDA) classifier was trained for each participant using all trials from all sessions (three sessions in Experiment 1, two sessions in Experiment 2) to discriminate target from no-target trials based on EEG data, irrespective of seen/unseen responses and irrespective of the response criterion.
evidence: This describes the neural data analysis method.

claim: A leave-one-person-out cross validated decoding scheme was applied to maximize signal-to-noise ratio.
source: To maximize signal-to-noise ratio, we applied a leave-one-person-out cross validated decoding scheme by using all classifiers from all participants except the participants that was being tested (separately for Experiment 1 and for Experiment 2).
evidence: This describes the cross-validation procedure used in the analysis.

claim: Classification was performed using occipitoparietal electrodes as these are most sensitive to the stimuli used.
source: We maximized signal-to-noise ratio by performing classification using occipitoparietal electrodes, as these are known to be most sensitive to these stimuli (Fahrenfort et al., 2017; Fahrenfort et al., 2008; Fahrenfort et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies showing electrode sensitivity.

claim: Three local maxima in classification performance occurred at 137, 266, and 430 ms.
source: We subsequently computed the average classification performance across both experiments (see Figure 3A, left panel) and identified three times at which local maxima occurred in this average (137, 266, and 430 ms).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A based on the neural data analysis.

claim: The three peaks in classification performance have highly similar topographic maps of current source density for both experiments.
source: Figure 3A (right panel) shows that these peaks have highly similar topographic maps of current source density, obtained from the forward transformed weights of the training data from the selected peaks for both experiments (Haufe et al., 2014).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A based on topographic analysis.

claim: Classification performance was higher for Experiment 1 than for Experiment 2.
source: Note that classification performance was higher for Experiment 1 than for Experiment 2, as this experiment had 3 sessions instead of 2, and target stimuli were presented for 40 ms instead of 30 ms (which also resulted in a higher behavioral d' for Experiment 1 than for Experiment 2).
evidence: This is based on comparison of neural decoding results between experiments.

claim: Trial counts were equated between liberal and conservative conditions within each participant to ensure differences could not be explained by disparities in signal-to-noise ratio.
source: To ensure that differences resulting from post hoc sorting could not be explained by differences in signal-to-noise ratio resulting from disparities in trial counts in the testing set, we equated trial counts between the liberal and conservative condition within each participant by randomly selecting the same number of trials from overrepresented cells (for Experiment 1, this was done at the level of 'seen' and 'unseen' responses, for Experiment 2 the trial counts were equated at each of the PAS levels, see methods for details).
evidence: This describes a methodological control in the analysis.

claim: A 2 (experiment) × 2 (visibility) × 2 (criterion) × 3 (latency) repeated measures ANOVA showed strong main effects of experiment, visibility, criterion, and latency.
source: We then entered these in a large 2 (experiment) × 2 (visibility) × 2 (criterion) × 3 (latency) repeated measures ANOVA with experiment as a between group factor. The result of this ANOVA showed strong main effects of experiment (Exp1 vs Exp2: F1,40 = 38.68, p < 10–6, η²p = 0.49), visibility (seen vs unseen: F1,40 = 204.01, p < 10–16, η²p = 0.84), criterion (liberal vs conservative: F1,40 = 20.98, p < 10–4, η²p = 0.34), and latency (137, 266, and 430 ms: F1.79,80 = 33.72, p < 10–8, η²p = 0.46), see Supplementary file 1a for the full ANOVA.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the neural decoding data.

claim: Post hoc sorting results in higher classification performance for the conservative than for the liberal condition.
source: These data confirm – as was predicted from our simulation – that post hoc sorting results in a large criterion effect, with higher classification performance for the conservative than for the liberal condition.
evidence: This is supported by the neural decoding results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Criterion did not significantly interact with experiment (F1,40 = 1.38, p = 0.25, η²p = 0.03).
source: The consistency of the effect is further supported by the fact that criterion did not significantly interact with experiment (F1,40 = 1.38, p = 0.25, η²p = 0.03).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the neural decoding data.

claim: Criterion interacted with visibility (F1,40 = 5.36, p = 0.026, η²p = 0.12).
source: Criterion did interact with visibility (F1,40 = 5.36, p = 0.026, η²p = 0.12), and with latency (F1.75,69.80 = 4.44, p = 0.02, η²p = 0.1), indicating that criterion effects on neural measures manifested differentially in different visibility levels and at different moments in time.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the neural decoding data.

claim: Criterion interacted with latency (F1.75,69.80 = 4.44, p = 0.02, η²p = 0.1).
source: Criterion did interact with visibility (F1,40 = 5.36, p = 0.026, η²p = 0.12), and with latency (F1.75,69.80 = 4.44, p = 0.02, η²p = 0.1), indicating that criterion effects on neural measures manifested differentially in different visibility levels and at different moments in time.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the neural decoding data.

claim: In both experiments, the criterion effect occurs at long latencies (266 and 430 ms) but not at the short latency of 137 ms.
source: Indeed, in both experiments the criterion effect occurs at long latencies (266 and 430 ms) but not at the short latency of 137 ms, as was established using one-sided t-tests (conservative >liberal) for simple effects in each of the three latencies for each of the two experiments (see Figure 3B, for the complete time courses of these experiments see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on post-hoc statistical tests shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There was a highly significant three-way interaction between criterion, experiment, and visibility (F1,40 = 18.47, p < 10–3, η²p = 0.32).
source: Finally, there was a highly significant three-way interaction between criterion, experiment, and visibility (F1,40 = 18.47, p < 10–3, η²p = 0.32), which we will expound on in much more detail further down below.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the neural decoding data.

claim: Without post hoc sorting, there was no main effect of criterion on classification performance (F1,40 = 1.16, p = 0.29, η²p = 0.03).
source: To test for criterion effects in the absence of post hoc sorting, we then entered these data in a 2 (experiment) × 2 (criterion) × 3 (latency) repeated measures ANOVA with experiment as a between group factor (naturally there was no factor visibility because there was no post hoc sorting). As before, the result of this ANOVA showed strong main effects of experiment (Exp1 vs Exp2: F1,40 = 28.45, p < 10–5, η²p=0.42), and latency (137, 266, and 430 ms: F1.70,67.95 = 49.95, p < 10–12, η²p = 0.56), but this time there was no main effect of criterion (liberal vs conservative: F1,40 = 1.16, p = 0.29, η²p = 0.03), see Supplementary file 1b for the full ANOVA.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of neural data without post hoc sorting.

claim: The criterion effects observed with post hoc sorting are due to post hoc sorting and not due to general effects of decoding sensitivity in the conservative versus liberal condition.
source: Figure 3C shows the effect of the criterion manipulation separately for the two experiments, with one-sided post hoc t-tests (conservative > liberal) for each of the three latencies. This figure shows that – if anything – the criterion effect is in the opposite direction of the effect observed in Figure 3B, further confirming that the criterion effects in Figure 3B are due to post hoc sorting and not due to general effects of decoding sensitivity in the conservative versus the liberal condition.
evidence: This is based on comparison of analyses with and without post hoc sorting shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: In Experiment 1, criterion strongly interacts with visibility (F1,15 = 11.06, p < 0.01, η²p = 0.42).
source: For Experiment 1, we performed a 2 (visibility) × 2 (criterion) × 3 (latency) repeated measures ANOVA (see Supplementary file 1c for the full ANOVA). This analysis again shows strong main effects of visibility (F1,15 = 81.38, p < 10–6, η²p = 0.84), criterion (F1,15 = 13.89, p < 0.01, η²p = 0.48), and latency (F2,30 = 37.13, p < 10–8, η²p = 0.71), but more importantly, it also shows that criterion strongly interacts with visibility in Experiment 1 (F1,15 = 11.06, p < 0.01, η²p = 0.42).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of Experiment 1 data.

claim: In Experiment 1, criterion effects were only significant in the 'unseen' condition but not in the 'seen' condition.
source: One-sided t-tests for simple effects (conservative > liberal) revealed that the criterion effects were only significant in the 'unseen' condition (Figure 4A, left panel), but not in the 'seen' condition (Figure 4A, right panel), and – as established before – that these effects only appear in the late 266/430 ms latencies as opposed to the early 137 ms latency.
evidence: This is based on post-hoc statistical tests shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In Experiment 2, criterion interacts with visibility (F2.29,41.37 = 2.86, p = 0.06, η²p = 0.10).
source: To investigate the interaction between visibility and criterion in Experiment 2, we performed the same analysis in a 4 (visibility) × 2 (criterion) × 3 (latency) repeated measures ANOVA, this time maintaining the four PAS responses as separate levels in the factor visibility (see Supplementary file 1d for the full ANOVA). Again, this analysis confirmed strong main effects of visibility (F2.37,59.22 = 67.29, p < 10–16, η²p = 0.73), criterion (F1,25 = 10.10, p = 0.004, η²p = 0.29), and latency (F1.89,47.28 = 13.26, p < 10–4, η²p = 0.35), as observed in Experiment 1. Moreover, this experiment-specific ANOVA confirms that here too, criterion interacts with visibility (F2.29,41.37 = 2.86, p = 0.06, η²p = 0.10).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of Experiment 2 data.

claim: In Experiment 2, criterion effects were predominantly in the 'seen' conditions of the PAS (PAS1, PAS2, and PAS3) but not in the 'unseen' condition (PAS0).
source: Post hoc t-tests for simple effects (conservative > liberal) revealed that in Experiment 2, the criterion effects were predominantly in the 'seen' conditions of the PAS (PAS1, PAS2, and PAS3, see Figure 4B, second, third, and fourth panels), but not in the 'unseen' condition (PAS0, see Figure 4B, leftmost panel), whereas Experiment 1 showed a significant effect in 'unseen' but not in 'seen' (and again only at late 266 and/or 430 ms latencies).
evidence: This is based on post-hoc statistical tests shown in Figure 4B.

claim: When sensitivity is low, a small criterion shift is more likely to have a large effect on the neural measure in the 'seen' condition after post hoc sorting.
source: First, we manipulated the degree of sensitivity (Figure 4C, D), while keeping the response thresholds for responding 'seen' or 'unseen' the same. When sensitivity is low (Figure 4C, left panels), a small criterion shift is more likely to have a large effect on the neural measure in the 'seen' condition after post hoc sorting (Figure 4C, right panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation results shown in Figure 4C.

claim: When sensitivity is high, a criterion shift is more likely to have a large effect on the 'unseen' condition.
source: Conversely, when sensitivity is high (Figure 4D, left panels) the same criterion shift is more likely to have a large effect on the 'unseen' condition (Figure 4D, right panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation results shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Under identical signal detection thresholds, a change in sensitivity can have a large differential impact on neural measures in 'seen' and 'unseen' conditions.
source: These simulations show that under identical signal detection thresholds, a change in sensitivity (e.g. when showing higher strength stimuli, or when an observer is more attentive), can have a large differential impact on the neural measures in 'seen' and 'unseen' conditions, making their interpretation intrinsically problematic.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results in Figure 4C and D.

claim: When the overall criterion is conservative, a small criterion shift might have a large effect on the neural measure in the 'seen' condition after post hoc sorting.
source: In a second simulation, we looked at the effect of overall criterion shifts (Figure 4E, F), while keeping sensitivity the same. When the overall criterion is conservative (Figure 4E, left panels), a small criterion shift might have a large effect on the neural measure in the 'seen' condition after post hoc sorting (Figure 4E, right panel), whereas when the overall criterion is liberal (Figure 4F, left panels) the same criterion shift can have a large effect in the 'unseen' condition (Figure 4F, right panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation results shown in Figure 4E.

claim: When the overall criterion is liberal, a criterion shift can have a large effect in the 'unseen' condition.
source: In a second simulation, we looked at the effect of overall criterion shifts (Figure 4E, F), while keeping sensitivity the same. When the overall criterion is conservative (Figure 4E, left panels), a small criterion shift might have a large effect on the neural measure in the 'seen' condition after post hoc sorting (Figure 4E, right panel), whereas when the overall criterion is liberal (Figure 4F, left panels) the same criterion shift can have a large effect in the 'unseen' condition (Figure 4F, right panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation results shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Small criterion shifts can have a differential impact on effect size in neural measures of 'seen' and 'unseen' stimuli depending on whether the overall criterion is liberal or conservative.
source: This shows that small criterion shifts can have a differential impact on the effect size in neural measures of 'seen' and 'unseen' stimuli, even when sensitivity stays the same, depending on whether the overall criterion is liberal or conservative, again making the interpretation of such effects problematic.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results in Figure 4E and F.

claim: Criterion shifts can differentially confound neural measures of conscious or unconscious processing depending on both overall criterion and sensitivity.
source: Thus, criterion shifts can differentially confound neural measures of conscious or unconscious processing, depending both on overall criterion and sensitivity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the simulation results.

claim: The direction of criterion influence on neural measures can be counterintuitive, is difficult to predict, and cannot be controlled experimentally.
source: The direction of this influence can be counterintuitive, is difficult to predict, and cannot be controlled experimentally.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation and empirical results.

claim: Experiment 1 has a much higher sensitivity than Experiment 2.
source: Interestingly, Experiment 1 has a much higher sensitivity than Experiment 2 (both in terms of classification accuracy and in terms of behavioral sensitivity, as pointed out before).
evidence: This is based on comparison of behavioral and neural measures between experiments.

claim: The difference in sensitivity between Experiments 1 and 2 provides a compelling explanation for why Experiment 1 shows the largest effect of criterion shift in the unseen condition while Experiment 2 shows it in the PAS1 condition and up.
source: This provides a compelling explanation for our finding that Experiment 1 (detection) shows the largest effect of the criterion shift in the unseen condition, whereas for Experiment 2 (PAS) the largest effect was observed in the PAS1 condition and up, which is nicely in line with the predictions from our simulation in Figure 4C, D.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the empirical results to the simulation predictions.

claim: Criterion and sensitivity either cannot be controlled in principle or are not controlled in practice.
source: Importantly, these factors either cannot be controlled in principle (criterion) and/or are not controlled in practice (sensitivity), which questions the construct validity of subjective measures under post hoc sorting.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the findings for experimental practice.

claim: Post hoc sorting on 'seen' and 'unseen' responses causes neural effect sizes to become stronger under a conservative compared to a liberal response criterion.
source: In this manuscript, we have shown through simulation that post hoc sorting on 'seen' and 'unseen' responses causes neural effect sizes in 'seen' and 'unseen' conditions to become stronger under a conservative compared to a liberal response criterion.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from simulations.

claim: Criterion shifts modulated effect size in neural measures of 'unconscious' and/or 'conscious' processing in both experiments.
source: To test this claim empirically, we analyzed data from two experiments in which criterion shifts were induced experimentally (one using a simple detection task, one using the PAS). We found that in both experiments, criterion shifts modulated effect size in neural measures of 'unconscious' (unseen) and/or 'conscious' (seen) processing, and that this happens even though the conservative and liberal condition used the same independent training data (identical classifiers), and even though the trial counts in the test sets were equated for the conservative and liberal condition.
evidence: This is a summary of the main empirical finding.

claim: Criterion shifts confound neural measures of conscious and unconscious processing under post hoc sorting.
source: Together, these data show that criterion shifts confound neural measures of conscious and unconscious processing under post hoc sorting.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the combined simulation and empirical results.

claim: Criterion shifts potentially contaminate studies of unconscious cognition.
source: Such confounds potentially contaminate studies of unconscious cognition (King et al., 2016; Soto et al., 2011) as well as studies that apply post hoc sorting to reveal neural measures of consciousness through a contrastive approach (van Boxtel et al., 2010; Hesselmann et al., 2011; Hesselmann and Malach, 2011; Levinson et al., 2021; Melloni et al., 2011; Ress and Heeger, 2003; Rolke et al., 2001; Salti et al., 2015; Sanchez et al., 2020; Sergent et al., 2005; Stein et al., 2021; van Vugt et al., 2018; Wyart and Tallon-Baudry, 2008).
evidence: This is an inference about the implications for prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: The contrast 'seen > unseen' can result in strong or weak differences between conditions depending on the response criterion adopted by observers.
source: Concretely, the contrast 'seen > unseen', used in neuroimaging studies to isolate the neural basis of consciousness, can either result in strong or in weak differences between conditions, depending on the response criterion that was adopted by the observers.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications for the interpretation of neural contrasts.

claim: Arbitrary criterion placement is intrinsic to decision making.
source: Unfortunately, arbitrary criterion placement is intrinsic to decision making, and is known to be affected by many factors that are not controlled between, or even within experiments.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about decision making.

claim: Context has a large effect on how observers place their criterion.
source: Context is known to have a large effect on how observers place their criterion. For example, the ratio of targets to non-targets (the base-rate), the strength of the target stimulus compared to noise (the signal-to-noise ratio), the utility of certain stimulus–response combinations (the payoff matrix), and even small changes in task instructions are all known to affect the response criterion (Fleming et al., 2010b; Kloosterman et al., 2019; Rakhshan et al., 2020; Supèr et al., 2001; White and Poldrack, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing contextual effects on criterion.

claim: The omnipresence of arbitrary criterion placement due to non-perceptual influences threatens the construct validity of subjective measures in consciousness research.
source: So even if some criterion shifts may have a perceptual origin (Meyerhoff and Scholl, 2018; Witt et al., 2015), the omnipresence of arbitrary criterion placement due to non-perceptual influences (Sánchez-Fuenzalida et al., 2023a; Sánchez-Fuenzalida et al., 2023b) threatens the construct validity of subjective measures in consciousness research.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications for subjective measures, supported by citations.

claim: Criterion shifts threaten the construct validity of the PAS.
source: Relatedly, criterion shifts also threaten the construct validity of the PAS.
evidence: This is an inference from the empirical results of Experiment 2.

claim: Experiment 2 shows that all levels of the PAS are sensitive to the criterion manipulation, even when explicitly instructing participants to only respond according to their experience.
source: Experiment 2 shows that all levels of the PAS are sensitive to the criterion manipulation, even when explicitly instructing participants to only respond according to their experience.
evidence: This is based on the behavioral results from Experiment 2.

claim: Both payoff and base-rate induced criterion shifts result in a bias on first order decisions and affect how second order confidence judgements are distributed.
source: This finding is in line with evidence showing similar effects on related subjective measures, such as confidence judgements. For example, both payoff and base-rate induced criterion shifts not only result in a bias on first order decisions, but also affect how second order confidence judgements are distributed (Lebreton et al., 2019; Lebreton et al., 2018; Locke et al., 2020), also see Peters et al., 2017.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on confidence judgments.

claim: Payoff and base-rate induced criterion shifts affect confidence scores even when perceptual experience is not affected.
source: Indeed, recent experiments from our lab have confirmed that payoff and base-rate induced criterion shifts affect confidence scores even when perceptual experience is not affected (Sánchez-Fuenzalida et al., 2023a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent work from the authors' lab.

claim: Any context influences the criterion in some way.
source: However, proper instruction does not resolve this issue. Any context – experimentally induced or not – influences the criterion in some way, and if there is no way to enforce that the adopted criterion is an unwavering threshold on subjective experience (and nothing else), any subjective measure is potentially prone to confounds of a non-experiental nature.
evidence: This is an inference about the fundamental problem with subjective measures.

claim: Without resolving the criterion problem, any experiment remains open to the critique that participants may not have adopted the subjective scale as intended.
source: Without resolving this, any experiment remains open to the critique that the participants in the study may not have adopted the subjective scale as it was intended, for whatever reason.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications for experimental validity.

claim: Criterion shifts are well known to occur without experimental manipulations and occur naturally across experiments with different ratios of target to non-targets and different overall levels of visibility.
source: Nevertheless, criterion shifts are well known to also occur without these manipulations and occur naturally across experiments that have different ratios of target to non-targets, different overall levels of visibility and so forth.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about criterion shifts.

claim: The current experiment can be viewed as a caricature of actual experimental practice.
source: As such, the current experiment can be viewed as a caricature of actual experimental practice.
evidence: This is a characterization of the experimental approach.

claim: There is no such thing as a criterion-free experimental context.
source: Importantly, there is no such thing as a criterion-free experimental context.
evidence: This is presented as a fundamental principle about experimental contexts.

claim: Many dimensions that are not controlled between experiments will have a large effect on the criterion even without manipulating it explicitly.
source: As pointed out in the beginning of this discussion and in our simulations, many dimensions that are not controlled between experiments, will have a large effect on the criterion even without manipulating it explicitly/experimentally.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation and empirical results.

claim: Many view subjective measures as a crucial behavioral marker of the presence or absence of consciousness.
source: Thus, researchers studying consciousness are faced with a difficult conundrum. On the one hand, many view subjective measures as a crucial behavioral marker of the presence or absence of consciousness (Baars, 1994; Dehaene, 2014; Overgaard et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to researchers advocating for subjective measures.

claim: Subjective measures do not reliably measure the construct they intend to measure due to criterion confounds.
source: On the other hand, subjective measures do not reliably measure the construct they intend to measure due to criterion confounds.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: Peters and Lau (2015) proposed combining an objective first order judgment with a criterion-free subjective measure by having participants place bets on their objective judgment.
source: A potential way out of this conundrum has been a proposal by Peters and Lau, 2015. They combined an objective, first order judgment with a criterion-free subjective measure by having participants place bets (as proxy for subjective reports) on their objective judgment.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Peters and Lau, 2015.

claim: In the Peters and Lau study, trials consisted of two intervals with only one containing a grating target, and subjects were asked to guess grating orientation for both intervals and place a bet on which judgment is more likely to be correct.
source: Trials consisted of two intervals, only one of them containing a grating target, and subjects were asked to guess grating orientation for both intervals and place a bet on which of these two judgments is deemed as more likely to be correct.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of Peters and Lau's study.

claim: Peters and Lau argued that above-chance objective performance in the absence of subjective insight measured in a criterion-free way would reflect unconscious perception.
source: They argued that above-chance objective performance in the absence of subjective insight measured in this criterion-free way would reflect unconscious perception.
evidence: This describes the theoretical argument of Peters and Lau.

claim: Saving the construct validity of subjective measures requires solving the criterion problem.
source: Without making any final judgment on this matter, we point out that saving the construct validity of subjective measures requires one to solve the criterion problem (Morgan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference about what is needed to address the validity issues, supported by a citation.

claim: Without a properly experimentally defined procedure for solving the criterion problem, the construct validity of subjective measures will remain under threat.
source: Without a properly experimentally defined procedure for doing so, their construct validity will remain under threat.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications for future research.

claim: Experimental contexts that induce conservative behavioral responses on subjective measures will overestimate neural correlates of both 'unconscious' and 'conscious' conditions.
source: Summarizing, aside from the effect of the criterion on behavioral responses themselves, we show both empirically and in simulation that post hoc trial sorting of neural data on subjective measures can have unintuitive consequences depending on the experimental context (i.e. depending on the criterion that participants adopt). Experimental contexts that induce conservative behavioral responses on subjective measures will overestimate estimates neural correlates of both 'unconscious' (unseen) and 'conscious' (seen) conditions, whereas experimental contexts that induce liberal behavioral responding do the reverse.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from simulations and empirical data.

claim: Experimental contexts that induce liberal behavioral responding will underestimate neural correlates of both 'unconscious' and 'conscious' conditions.
source: Summarizing, aside from the effect of the criterion on behavioral responses themselves, we show both empirically and in simulation that post hoc trial sorting of neural data on subjective measures can have unintuitive consequences depending on the experimental context (i.e. depending on the criterion that participants adopt). Experimental contexts that induce conservative behavioral responses on subjective measures will overestimate estimates neural correlates of both 'unconscious' (unseen) and 'conscious' (seen) conditions, whereas experimental contexts that induce liberal behavioral responding do the reverse.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from simulations and empirical data.
